summary: A court romance of desire, jealousy, loneliness, and the sadness of things, in which love is shadowed by guilt, shame, and loss.

need-to-breathe.why: No character struggles for breath; even Ukifune's attempt to drown herself in the Uji river is told after the fact.

hungry.why: Ōigimi refuses food and wastes away at Uji, but otherwise meals are court background that the tale passes over.

gassy.why: Intestinal gas has no place in the tale.

sleepy.why: Lovers' nights and dawn partings fill the tale, and Genji lies sleepless after Murasaki's death, but sleep as a bodily need is never pressing.

nauseous.why: No character sickens from food; Fujitsubo's pregnancy indisposition is mentioned only to hide the child's timing.

dizzy.why: Genji's fever drives him to the Kitayama healer, and Aoi and Murasaki collapse under spirit attacks, but dizziness itself is barely noted.

fatigued.why: The characters are courtiers who ride in carriages and compose poems; exertion to the point of fatigue plays no part.

pain.why: Aoi suffers a possessed labor and Murasaki's final illness drags on for months, but bodily pain is rarely described directly.

disgusted.why: Genji recoils from Suetsumuhana's long red nose and from the amorous, aged Gen no Naishi, though he still courts both out of pity and curiosity.

over-stimulated.why: Court music and incense please rather than overwhelm; no sense is ever assaulted.

too-hot-too-cold.why: Suitors wait out cold nights behind blinds, snow falls on Rokujō's garden and Suetsumuhana's ruined house, and the sea storm at Suma soaks Genji's exile.

afraid.why: Genji is terrified when a spirit kills Yūgao in the deserted villa, Rokujō's living spirit strikes Aoi and Murasaki, and Ukifune lives in dread of her two lovers meeting.

anxious.why: Fujitsubo and Genji dread that their secret son Reizei will be discovered, Kashiwagi sickens with fear after Genji learns of his affair, and Ukifune frets between Kaoru and Niou.

panic.why: Genji's household panics in the dark villa when Yūgao dies, and Ukifune, trapped between two lovers, flees in the night toward the Uji river.

sensory-pleasures.why: Incense contests, koto and flute music, moonlit gardens, layered silks, and the seasons at Rokujō are savored by Genji and his ladies.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: Poems exchanged at every meeting, the picture contest, calligraphy judged as character, Genji's Blue Sea Waves dance, and Rokujō's four seasonal gardens make art the texture of life.

fun-excitement.why: The cherry blossom banquet, the picture contest, and the kemari game at which Kashiwagi glimpses the Third Princess give the court its diversions.

orgasm.why: Genji's liaisons with Utsusemi, Yūgao, Oborozukiyo, and others are consummated behind curtains, with the act itself passed over in a line.

love-romantic.why: Genji's lifelong love for Murasaki, his forbidden passion for Fujitsubo, and Kaoru's and Niou's rivalry over the Uji sisters and Ukifune make courtship the tale's substance.

love-family.why: The Kiritsubo Emperor dotes on Genji, Genji raises the Akashi daughter to be empress, and the Eighth Prince's dying charge to his daughters shapes the Uji chapters.

grief.why: Genji mourns Yūgao, Aoi, Fujitsubo, and finally Murasaki, after whose death he spends a year in grief before his own; Kaoru mourns Ōigimi.

missing-someone.why: Genji in exile at Suma pines for Murasaki, the Akashi Lady gives up her daughter and yearns for her, and Genji's longing for his lost mother shapes every love.

aroused-sexually.why: Genji's desire drives him to Utsusemi's bedchamber, to Oborozukiyo, and to Fujitsubo, and Niou's appetite sends him to Nakanokimi and Ukifune.

liking-as-a-friend.why: Genji and Tō no Chūjō spar in the rainy-night discussion of women and remain lifelong friends and rivals, as Kaoru and Niou are a generation later.

empathy.why: Genji is admired for feeling others' sorrows, Murasaki quietly reads the pain of the women around her, and Kaoru is moved by the Uji sisters' plight.

compassion.why: Genji provides for the destitute Suetsumuhana and takes in the orphaned Murasaki and Tamakazura, and the Bishop of Yokawa saves the half-drowned Ukifune.

grateful.why: Suetsumuhana and the Akashi family owe Genji their standing and feel it, and the exiled Genji thanks the Akashi novice for shelter.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Genji takes pleasure in installing his ladies at Rokujō and advancing their fortunes, and in raising Murasaki to his ideal.

trustful-distrustful.why: Murasaki learns to distrust Genji's assurances when he marries the Third Princess, Genji reads Kashiwagi's letter and knows Kaoru is not his, and Ukifune hides Niou from Kaoru.

depressed.why: Ōigimi turns her face to the wall and starves, Ukifune walks to the river in despair, and Genji after Murasaki's death withdraws from the world.

angry.why: Rokujō's humiliation at the carriage fight turns to spirit-wrath against Aoi, and Genji's cold anger drives Kashiwagi to his sickbed.

envious.why: Court women envy the favor shown to Genji's mother, and Rokujō's humiliation when Aoi's carriage shoves hers aside at the Kamo festival breeds the envy that kills.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: Rokujō's jealous spirit kills Yūgao and Aoi and attacks Murasaki, Murasaki pines over the Akashi Lady and the Third Princess, and Niou rages at Kaoru's visits to Ukifune.

jealous-friendship.why: Tō no Chūjō and Genji compete in dance, poetry, and women, but their rivalry is for status more than for each other's regard.

hatred.why: The Kokiden Consort and her father hate Genji as a threat to their line and seize on the Oborozukiyo affair to drive him into exile at Suma.

contempt.why: Genji sneers at Suetsumuhana's old-fashioned robes and verses, and the court looks down on the Akashi Lady's provincial birth.

resentment.why: Murasaki quietly resents each new wife and mistress Genji installs, and Rokujō resents the public slight of the carriage fight and Genji's neglect.

proud.why: Genji is vain of his beauty and accomplishments, rank obsesses every character, and Genji glories in seeing his Akashi daughter made empress.

amused.why: Genji paints his own nose red to tease little Murasaki after seeing Suetsumuhana, and the young men's rainy-night tales of women are told for laughs.

sense-of-belonging.why: Genji's exile at Suma strips him of his place at court until his triumphant return, and Ukifune, a provincial governor's stepdaughter, never belongs among the princes.

lonely.why: Genji in exile at Suma, Suetsumuhana forgotten in her overgrown mansion, Murasaki alone at Rokujō, and Ukifune isolated at Uji all suffer loneliness.

judgy-moral-sense.why: Genji's affair with Fujitsubo is a sin he fears will bring karmic punishment, the court condemns his liaison with Oborozukiyo, and Genji judges Kashiwagi as he was once judged.

admiration.why: Everyone, from the emperor to serving women, marvels at the Shining Genji's beauty, dancing, and poems, and Kaoru's natural fragrance is admired at court.

embarrassed.why: Genji is caught in Oborozukiyo's rooms by her father, and Suetsumuhana's awkward gift of an old-fashioned robe makes Genji wince for her.

shame.why: Kashiwagi wastes to death after Genji's barbed toast exposes his affair, Fujitsubo takes vows to bury her shame, and Ukifune would rather drown than be exposed.

guilt.why: Genji and Fujitsubo carry the guilt of deceiving the Emperor with Reizei, Kashiwagi is crushed by guilt over the Third Princess, and Genji reads Kaoru's birth as his own sin returned.

sad.why: The sadness of things pervades every chapter, from the Kiritsubo Emperor's loss to Genji's autumn of mourning and Kaoru's unanswered longing at Uji.

happy.why: Genji's years at Rokujō, with his ladies gathered in the four seasonal quarters and his daughter rising at court, are a brief fullness before loss.

joyful-euphoric.why: Genji's recall from Suma and the Akashi daughter's bearing a crown prince bring bursts of triumph.

effort.why: Kaoru's slow courtship of the Uji sisters and Genji's years of waiting for Fujitsubo are patient rather than strenuous; effort is hardly felt.

focused-in-flow.why: Genji loses himself in painting the shore at Suma and in koto playing, and the court's musicians and calligraphers are shown absorbed in their art.

bored.why: Genji's days at Suma stretch empty, and the women of Rokujō wait through tedious seasons for visits that rarely come.

distracted.why: Kashiwagi cannot attend to anything after glimpsing the Third Princess, and Genji's affairs keep pulling his mind from court and from Murasaki.

impatient.why: Niou cannot wait to get to Ukifune at Uji through the snow, and Genji chafes through the years until Murasaki is old enough.

curious.why: Genji peeps through fences to discover hidden ladies, the rainy-night talk sets him hunting for women of the middle rank, and Kaoru searches out the secret of his birth.

surprised.why: Genji is startled to find Kashiwagi's letter in the Third Princess's rooms, Kaoru is stunned to learn his true father, and Ukifune is found alive at Ono.

awe.why: Genji's Blue Sea Waves dance moves the court to tears, and the storm at Suma, followed by his father's ghost in a dream, is felt as the gods' intervention.

skeptical-doubtful.why: Genji doubts the Third Princess's child is his until the letter proves it, Murasaki doubts his vows, and Kaoru suspects Niou has reached Ukifune.

feeling-of-knowing.why: Kaoru senses a secret in his birth before the old nun tells it, and Genji half-recognizes Fujitsubo in the child Murasaki's face.

confused.why: Ukifune, rescued from the river, cannot remember who she is, and Genji cannot understand the spirit that struck Yūgao dead.

frustrated.why: Utsusemi slips away leaving her robe, Asagao refuses Genji for life, Ōigimi refuses Kaoru until death, and the tale ends with Ukifune refusing to see him.

uncertain-certain.why: Ukifune cannot choose between Kaoru and Niou, Genji wavers over the Third Princess, and Murasaki debates taking vows against Genji's refusal.

understanding.why: Genji comes to understand the Third Princess affair as retribution for his own sin against his father, and Kaoru finally understands who he is.

inspired.why: Poems come to lovers in an instant, and Genji conceives the four-season Rokujō mansion as a place for all his ladies.

satisfied.why: Genji sees his plans for the Akashi daughter fulfilled, but the tale closes unresolved, with Kaoru turned away from Ukifune's door.

foreboding.why: A Korean physiognomist foretells Genji's troubled greatness, his dead father appears in a dream before his recall, and Murasaki senses her end approaching.

nostalgia.why: Genji seeks his dead mother in Fujitsubo and Fujitsubo in Murasaki, sorts Murasaki's old letters after her death, and the later court looks back on the Shining Prince.

anticipation-suspense.why: Women wait through the night listening for Genji's carriage, and the secret of Reizei's birth hangs over Genji and Fujitsubo for years.

hope.why: The Akashi novice stakes everything on his daughter's union with Genji, the exile hopes for recall, and the women of Rokujō hope for a visit.

schadenfreude.why: The Kokiden faction relishes Genji's fall into exile, but gloating is a rare note in a tale of regret.

elevation.why: Genji's continued care for the ugly, impoverished Suetsumuhana, and the Bishop of Yokawa's kindness to Ukifune, are the tale's moments of moral grace.

infatuation.why: Genji's obsession with Fujitsubo, Kashiwagi's fatal fixation on the Third Princess, and Niou's infatuation with Ukifune drive the plot.

rage.why: Rokujō's spirit, speaking through Aoi's possessed body, screams its rage at Genji; otherwise fury is muted by courtly restraint.
